In the municipal office in Kalimpong, Dolma had found a mistake in last month's water report: two wards swapped. The fix was simple. The email to the district engineer was maybe six lines. But it meant admitting that she had signed off on the wrong numbers.
On Tuesday she opened a draft and typed "Respected Sir." Then she went for tea.
On Wednesday she tidied the file cupboard, all of it.
On Thursday she answered every other email in her inbox, even ones from last year.
Her colleague Jaya watched her rearrange her pens for the third time. "Dolma, what are you not doing?"
Dolma laughed, but her chest felt tight. "One email."
"How long will it take?"
"Five minutes. It's been three days."
Jaya pulled up a chair. "Then let's do the five minutes."

qa.q: What was the mistake Dolma found in the water report?
qa.a: Two wards had been swapped.

qa.q: Why did Dolma tidy cupboards and answer old emails instead?
qa.a: She felt anxious and ashamed about admitting she signed off wrong numbers, so any other task felt easier than facing that feeling.

The email to Kofi's thesis supervisor was simple: I'm going to miss the chapter deadline; can we move it two weeks? Three sentences. He had known he needed to send it since Monday.
By Thursday evening in their Leeds flat, he had cleaned the oven, reorganised his bookshelf by colour and started learning to juggle.
Selin found him in the kitchen with three oranges. "You sent it?"
"I'm about to."
"You said that yesterday."
He put the oranges down. "She's going to think I'm not serious. She'll be disappointed. She might say no."
"She might. Or she might say fine."
"It's three sentences, Selin. Why is it so hard?"
"Because the three sentences are carrying a lot of feelings."
He opened the laptop, read the draft again, and finally pressed send. Then he sat very still, waiting for the reply.

qa.a: He cleaned the oven, reorganised his bookshelf by colour and started learning to juggle.

Team lead's note, research office — Mahima
Parveen had not touched the grant progress report for nine days. On Monday I found her staring at the blank file. She said, "I'm so useless. Everyone else finished weeks ago." She looked close to tears, and I noticed that every time she scolded herself, she closed the file again.
I told her that delays happen, that she was not in trouble, and that we would only ask for five minutes. "Just open it and write the headings. That's all today."
She did. Five minutes turned into forty. By the afternoon she had a rough first section.
On Wednesday she told me she had started saying to herself, "Okay, you're late. That's human. Five minutes." She finished the report on Friday.
I will offer the same approach to the new team members.

Sunday, 11 p.m.
Three weeks since I last touched my portfolio website. I'm Saurabh, and the old routine is: open laptop, see the mess, call myself lazy, close laptop, feel terrible, avoid it for another week.
Today Lokesh came over and saw the folder on my desktop called "PORTFOLIO FINAL FINAL." He didn't laugh. He said, "You know you're allowed to just be late? Try five minutes. Not fixing it. Just looking."
So after he left, I said it out loud, a bit embarrassed: "You're late, and that's okay. Five minutes." Set a timer.
I uploaded one project photo. Then another. The timer went off and I didn't notice.
Forty minutes. Three projects up.
It's strange. Calling myself lazy never got a single page done. Being kind got three.

qa.a: Saurabh uploaded three projects.

qa.a: Saurabh felt a bit embarrassed saying it, but it eased the guilt enough to start.

qa.a: Being kind removed the guilt that fed avoidance, and five minutes was small enough to begin; once started, Saurabh kept going for forty minutes.

qa.a: Lokesh would probably feel glad and a little proud that the gentle suggestion to be allowed to be late actually helped.

Still, when the old clock in the hall struck nine, Sunaina put down her flower petals, went to the back verandah and picked up her toothbrush without being told. Her aunt Aparna, visiting from Chennai, watched in surprise.
"Doesn't anyone have to call you?"
Sunaina shrugged, foam on her lips. "It's nine."
After brushing, she went straight to Ammamma's room and lay down on the mat. Ammamma began the story of the clever crow, the same one she told every night. Before the crow found the pebbles, Sunaina was asleep, one hand still curled around a petal.
Aparna smiled. In the city, her own son fought bedtime every night.

The long rains had come to Addis Ababa, and the power went out most evenings. Abebe's neighbour Rosa, who looked after him while his parents worked late, expected bedtime to be a battle in the dark.
But at eight, when the church bell down the road rang, Abebe got up from the floor without a word. He found the torch on the shelf, brushed his teeth at the basin by its light and climbed into bed.
"Story, Rosa," he said. "The one about the monkey and the market."
Rosa told it, rain drumming on the tin roof. Halfway through, Abebe's breathing slowed.
She sat there a while, surprised. No arguing, no "five more minutes." The bell, the brush, the story, then sleep, one step pulling the next, even with no lights at all.

Kamal raised his eyebrows. She looked at the screen time and felt her face go hot. Two hours, in pieces of two minutes.

The first three times I tried to start running, I lasted four days each. I'm Arohi, second-year BSc, and my plan was always big: five kilometres, six a.m., every day. By day four I'd wake up, think about the whole five kilometres and roll over.
